topic: Sir Creek and six more borders that make no sense
hook: Your map of Gujarat ends in a border that runs through mud, and two countries still cannot agree where it is.
title: Sir Creek and 6 Borders That Make No Sense
description:
Seven real borders that make no sense, counted down from a lake with no line to a rocket city that Russia rents. The last one is India's Sir Creek, a border in a tidal marsh where the water keeps moving and India and Pakistan still disagree on where the line lies. Open any map and check them yourself.

#borders #geography #India

scenes.narration: Your map of Gujarat ends in a border that runs through mud, and two countries still cannot agree where it is.
scenes.headline: A Border In Mud

scenes.narration: That is Sir Creek, India's strangest border, and we will get there last. But six others come first, and each is stranger.
scenes.headline: Sir Creek Comes Last

scenes.narration: By the end, you will see a line on a map that the water itself keeps moving.
scenes.headline: A Line That Moves

scenes.narration: Here are seven real borders that make no sense, counted down from seven to one, starting with a lake that has no line.
scenes.headline: 7 Real Borders

scenes.narration: Every place in this video is real, and every one is on a map you can open right now.
scenes.headline: All Real, All On Maps

scenes.narration: So let us start with a border that was simply never drawn, in the middle of rich, careful Europe.
scenes.headline: Never Drawn

scenes.narration: Number seven: a lake with no agreed border. Lake Constance touches three countries, Germany, Austria and Switzerland, all careful and well organised.
scenes.headline: Lake With No Border

scenes.narration: On land, their borders are clear. But out on the water, the three have never agreed on one shared line.
scenes.headline: No Line On Water

scenes.narration: Their views differ, so for decades the lake has been used by all three without a fixed line.
scenes.headline: Three Views

scenes.narration: Ferries cross it all day, boats of all three nations sail it, and nobody checks a passport in the middle of the water.
scenes.headline: No Passport Checks

scenes.narration: Think about that. An entire lake, in the middle of Europe, with the border left as a blank on the map.
scenes.headline: A Blank On The Map

scenes.narration: Fishing and shipping rules there are agreed between the neighbours, even without a border line.
scenes.headline: Rules, No Line

scenes.narration: That one is just a blank. Number six is much stranger: a whole town stuck in the wrong country.
scenes.headline: Next: Wrong Country

scenes.narration: Number six: Llívia. It is a Spanish town that sits completely inside French land, with France on every side.
scenes.headline: Spain Inside France

scenes.narration: Walk out of the town in any direction and you step onto French soil. Spain is only a short drive away.
scenes.headline: Step Out, Step Into France

scenes.narration: The reason goes back to 1659, when Spain handed France a set of villages after a long war, in the Treaty of the Pyrenees.
scenes.headline: The 1659 Treaty

scenes.narration: But Llívia was counted as a town, not a village. So it was not handed over, and it stayed Spanish.
scenes.headline: Town, Not Village

scenes.narration: One word on a piece of paper left a Spanish town stranded inside France, and it is still there.
scenes.headline: One Word Did It

scenes.narration: Today a special road joins Llívia to the rest of Spain, and that road runs through French land.
scenes.headline: A Road Through France

scenes.narration: That is a town inside the wrong country. Number five is a village, and it is surrounded by Switzerland.
scenes.headline: Next: A Swiss Island

scenes.narration: Number five: Büsingen. It is a village in Germany, but it is completely surrounded by Switzerland.
scenes.headline: Germany Inside Switzerland

scenes.narration: Its people live under German law, yet it sits inside the Swiss customs area, so goods move there much like in Switzerland.
scenes.headline: German Law, Swiss Customs

scenes.narration: Shops there often take both euros and Swiss francs, because both currencies are part of daily life.
scenes.headline: Euros And Francs

scenes.narration: Its cars have their own special number plate code, BÜS, so you can spot a Büsingen car at a glance.
scenes.headline: Plate Code: BÜS

scenes.narration: Old land deals and old wars left it behind, and nobody ever tidied it away. It still sits on the map as a German island in Swiss land.
scenes.headline: A German Island

scenes.narration: Imagine your home address being German, while everything you can see from your window is Switzerland.
scenes.headline: German Address, Swiss View

scenes.narration: That one was about land. Number four is about a runway, and what happens when a plane wants to land.
scenes.headline: Next: A Runway

scenes.narration: Number four: Gibraltar. A British territory on Spain's southern tip, with a border that runs right across its airport.
scenes.headline: Border Over A Runway

scenes.narration: To walk or drive from Spain into Gibraltar, you often have to cross the airport runway itself.
scenes.headline: You Cross The Runway

scenes.narration: When a plane is about to land or take off, the road is closed. Barriers come down, just like at a railway crossing.
scenes.headline: Barriers Come Down

scenes.narration: Cars, bikes and people simply wait, while a jet lands or lifts off right in front of them.
scenes.headline: Wait For The Jet

scenes.narration: Few places on Earth have a border crossing where the plane has the right of way.
scenes.headline: Planes Go First

scenes.narration: Spain does not even accept that the land under the runway belongs to Gibraltar, so the argument is literally on the tarmac.
scenes.headline: A Dispute On Tarmac

scenes.narration: Number three is a place that is American, but to drive there, you must first pass through another country.
scenes.headline: Next: Drive Through Canada

scenes.narration: Number three: Point Roberts, in Washington state. It is part of the United States, but it hangs off the coast of Canada.
scenes.headline: America Cut Off

scenes.narration: The border follows the 49th parallel, a perfectly straight line, and that line sliced the tip of a peninsula off from America.
scenes.headline: The 49th Parallel

scenes.narration: So to reach the rest of the United States by road, you must drive through Canada and cross the border twice.
scenes.headline: Cross Twice To Get Home

scenes.narration: On the map it looks like a small cut-out of America, sitting just below Canada, with the sea on its other sides.
scenes.headline: A Small Cut-Out

scenes.narration: Its shops, its mail and many of its visitors all depend on a single crossing. When the border closed in 2020, the town felt it badly.
scenes.headline: One Crossing Matters

scenes.narration: A straight line drawn on a map long ago, by people who never needed to drive that road.
scenes.headline: A Line On Paper

scenes.narration: Now, number two is a city that is not in Russia, though Russia runs it, and it sends people into space.
scenes.headline: Next: A Rented City

scenes.narration: Number two: Baikonur. It is a city inside Kazakhstan that is leased to and run by Russia.
scenes.headline: A City Russia Rents

scenes.narration: It is where Yuri Gagarin's rocket lifted off in 1961, and it is still a working launch site today.
scenes.headline: Gagarin Started Here

scenes.narration: The land belongs to Kazakhstan, but Russia pays rent to use it, and the Russian space programme runs the launches.
scenes.headline: Russia Pays Rent

scenes.narration: So you can stand in Kazakhstan, and watch a Russian rocket carry astronauts to the space station.
scenes.headline: Kazakh Soil, Russian Rocket

scenes.narration: Entering the city comes with its own rules, and visitors need permission, even though it sits inside Kazakhstan.
scenes.headline: Permission Needed

scenes.narration: If you like strange places like these, subscribe, because we find a new one every single day.
scenes.headline: New Strange Place Daily

scenes.narration: A whole city, rented out like a flat, and rockets leave from it. Strange, but there is one left.
scenes.headline: Rented Like A Flat

scenes.narration: Number one is in India, close to home, and it is a border where you cannot even see the line.
scenes.headline: Number One Is Indian

scenes.narration: Number one: Sir Creek. On your map of Gujarat's far west, a border runs straight into a tidal marsh.
scenes.headline: Sir Creek

scenes.narration: Sir Creek is a long, narrow channel of water, where the Rann of Kutch meets the Arabian Sea.
scenes.headline: Where Marsh Meets Sea

scenes.narration: On one side is Gujarat, in India. On the other side is Sindh, in Pakistan.
scenes.headline: Gujarat Meets Sindh

scenes.narration: But this is not a neat river with two clear banks. It is a maze of mud flats, reeds and salt water.
scenes.headline: No Clear Banks

scenes.narration: Twice a day the tide floods the marsh, then drains it, and the shape of the channels keeps changing.
scenes.headline: Tide In, Tide Out

scenes.narration: Silt builds up, channels shift, and a patch of mud can appear in one season and vanish in another.
scenes.headline: Mud Appears, Vanishes

scenes.narration: Now try drawing a permanent line through that. That is the whole problem, and it has lasted for decades.
scenes.headline: A Permanent Line?

scenes.narration: The story starts before 1947. This land was split between Kutch, a princely state, and Sindh, a province of British India.
scenes.headline: Kutch And Sindh

scenes.narration: In 1914 the Bombay government settled a dispute between them, with a resolution, and maps to go with it.
scenes.headline: The 1914 Resolution

scenes.narration: Pakistan reads those papers as putting the line on the eastern edge of the creek, which would make the whole channel Pakistani.
scenes.headline: Pakistan: East Bank

scenes.narration: India reads them differently. It says the line runs down the middle of the channel, and points to a 1925 map with pillars set along it.
scenes.headline: India: Mid-Channel

scenes.narration: There is even a name for that idea, the thalweg: a border that follows the middle of the main channel.
scenes.headline: The Thalweg Rule

scenes.narration: Pakistan argues that rule applies only to waterways that ships really use, and says this creek is not one of them.
scenes.headline: Is It Navigable?

scenes.narration: Both sides have a serious argument. It all comes down to which part of a muddy channel the line sits in.
scenes.headline: Which Side Of Mud?

scenes.narration: In 1965 the two countries clashed in the nearby Rann of Kutch, and a tribunal later ruled on that area in 1968.
scenes.headline: The 1968 Ruling

scenes.narration: But Sir Creek was not settled by that ruling, so it stayed open, and it is still open today.
scenes.headline: Still Not Settled

scenes.narration: Talks have gone on for decades, and the line has still not been agreed by both countries.
scenes.headline: Decades Of Talks

scenes.narration: And because the channels shift, the question gets harder every year. Which channel was the creek, and where is its middle now?
scenes.headline: Where Is The Middle?

scenes.narration: Fishermen feel it most. These waters are full of fish, and boats from both sides can drift across a line nobody can see.
scenes.headline: Fishermen Feel It

scenes.narration: Gujarat fishermen have often been arrested by Pakistan, and Pakistani fishermen by India, for crossing a line that was never clear.
scenes.headline: Arrested Over A Line

scenes.narration: Border guards patrol in boats, through salt flats and tidal water where there is very little except mud and sky.
scenes.headline: Patrols In Mud

scenes.narration: And it matters far beyond mud. Where the creek line ends helps decide where the sea border starts.
scenes.headline: It Sets The Sea Border

scenes.narration: That means one muddy bend, barely visible on a map, shapes who controls a large patch of the Arabian Sea.
scenes.headline: One Bend, Big Sea

scenes.narration: That is why this is India's strangest border. It is not a wall or a fence, just a line that moves with the water.
scenes.headline: A Line That Moves

scenes.narration: So remember where we started: your map of Gujarat ends in a border that runs through mud.
scenes.headline: A Border In Mud

scenes.narration: Seven borders, and not one of them makes sense. But the last one cannot even sit still.
scenes.headline: Seven Borders, Zero Sense

scenes.narration: Next video: a place where your phone picks up a signal from the wrong country.
scenes.headline: Next: Wrong Signal
